result.summary: Dido, in love with Æneas, is encouraged by her sister Anna, and Juno and Venus arrange a union in a cave during a hunting storm. Jove sends Mercury to order Æneas to sail for Italy; he leaves despite Dido's pleas and curses, and she kills herself on a pyre.

scenes.title: Dido confides in Anna
scenes.summary: Dido admits her love for Æneas but recalls her vow to Sychæus. Anna urges her to marry and persuades her.
scenes.stakes: Dido risks her honour, her vow to Sychæus and her city's safety by yielding to love.

scenes.title: Dido's love-madness
scenes.summary: Dido offers sacrifices, wanders the city like a wounded doe, and hangs on Æneas's tales. Building at Carthage stops.
scenes.stakes: Dido's mind and her city's progress are consumed by passion.

scenes.title: Juno and Venus bargain
scenes.summary: Juno proposes a shared rule and a marriage; Venus doubts but agrees. Juno plans a storm during the hunt.
scenes.stakes: Juno's favourite city and Venus's Trojans, and the future of Italy, are in tension.

scenes.title: The hunt and the cave
scenes.summary: The hunting party rides out; a storm scatters it and Dido and Æneas shelter in a cave, where Dido calls it marriage.

scenes.title: Fame and Iarbas
scenes.summary: Fame spreads the rumour and Iarbas prays to Jove in anger.
scenes.stakes: Dido faces scandal and the hostility of neighbouring rulers.

scenes.title: Mercury's message
scenes.summary: Jove sends Mercury, who flies past Atlas and rebukes Æneas.
scenes.stakes: Æneas's destiny, and Ascanius's inheritance of Italy, are at risk.

scenes.title: Dido confronts Æneas
scenes.summary: Æneas secretly prepares to leave; Dido learns of it and reproaches him, and he replies that Italy is his duty.
scenes.stakes: Dido stands to lose her lover and her fame; Æneas risks angering Jove and abandoning his destiny.

scenes.title: Curses and Anna's embassy
scenes.summary: Dido curses Æneas and leaves. The Trojans launch their ships, and Anna carries Dido's pleas in vain.
scenes.stakes: Dido begs for a little time to avoid death.

scenes.title: Omens and the false pyre
scenes.summary: Dido sees omens, tricks Anna into building a pyre for magic rites, and agonises at night.

scenes.title: Æneas sails away
scenes.summary: Mercury warns Æneas again in a dream, and he cuts the cables and sails.
scenes.stakes: Æneas and his fleet face Dido's wrath if they delay.

scenes.title: Dido's death
scenes.summary: Dido sees the fleet depart, curses Æneas and his descendants, and stabs herself on the pyre. Iris cuts her lock of hair to free her soul.

alias_notes.explanation: Another name of the Carthaginian queen.
Latin names for the king of the gods used interchangeably.
Mercury was born on Mount Cyllene.

notable_quotes.reason: Foreshadows the tragedy that follows the cave union.
Famous apostrophe on the power of love.
Mercury's often-quoted line on woman's fickleness.

analysis.text: Duty against passion: Æneas's destiny in Italy collides with Dido's love, and her tragedy becomes the origin of Rome's enmity with Carthage.
Dido's curse of eternal enmity explains the Punic Wars in myth, written for Augustan Rome.

legacy.text: Dido's story inspired Marlowe's Dido, Queen of Carthage (c. 1590) and Purcell's opera Dido and Æneas (c. 1689).
Virgil's personification of Fame shaped later allegories of rumour, as in Chaucer's House of Fame.

fun_facts.text: Virgil's tale of Dido's love for Æneas is likely his own invention; earlier traditions made her remain faithful to her husband.

language_notes.text: "The dawn-goddess" is Aurora, and "Phœbus' torch" is the sun, so the line simply means morning had come.
Dido means a base soul shows itself through cowardice, so Æneas's bearing proves him noble and probably descended from gods.
"Made me the dupe of death" means her first husband's death deceived her hopes and left her bereaved. "This one reproach" is Dido's wording for yielding to this one temptation.
Her brother Pygmalion murdered Sychæus at the household altar, so the "gods of my home" were sprinkled with his blood.
Erebus is the dark region of the underworld where the dead go. The "all-powerful sire" is Jupiter, who hurls thunderbolts.
Iarbas was a Libyan king whose suit Dido had refused. Tyre is the Phœnician city she fled.
These are the hostile peoples and places of North Africa around Carthage: Gætulians, Numidians, the Syrtis (a dangerous gulf of shoals) and the nation of Barce.
Orion's setting and rising was associated with storms at sea, so Anna uses it to suggest winter weather will keep the Trojans in port.
Ceres the lawgiver, Phœbus (Apollo) and Lyæus (Bacchus, god of wine) receive sacrifice; Juno is honored most as goddess of marriage, which hints at Dido's wish.
The narrator interrupts: the seers (priests reading entrails) cannot see the real cause of her trouble, which is love, not divine displeasure.
Dicte is a mountain in Crete; the Cretan woods were famous for hunting and archery.
The wealth of Sidon: Dido came from Tyre, and Sidon was a neighboring Phoenician city; the name stands for Phoenician riches.
Juno speaks ironically: the 'praise' and 'spoils' mock Venus and Cupid for needing two gods to conquer one woman.
Phrygian means Trojan; Phrygia was the region of Asia Minor associated with Troy. Tyrians are Dido's people.
Hymen is the god of marriage, invoked at weddings.
"Toils" are hunting nets; "chivalry" here simply means mounted riders, and Massylians were North African horsemen from Numidia.
"Punic" means Carthaginian; a "palfrey" is a saddle horse.
"Tyrian" means purple-dyed or from Tyre, Dido's original home; the scarf is edged with embroidery.
"Phrygian" here means Trojan; Iulus is Ascanius, Æneas' son.
"Dardania" is Troy's region, named for the ancestor Dardanus; "hope of Dardania" refers to Ascanius as heir of the Trojans.
Earth and Juno, goddess of marriage, act as ritual presiders over the union, a mock wedding with no human witnesses.
The lightning serves as wedding torches and the nymphs' cries as the wedding hymn, but these are ominous substitutes.
"Screen of her sin" means she uses the word marriage to cover what others would condemn; the narrator judges her.
Cœus and Enceladus were Titans and Giants who fought the gods; Fame, as Earth's youngest child, belongs to that rebellious family.
Ammon is the Libyan form of Jove (Jupiter Ammon); Iarbas claims the god as father by a Garamantian nymph, a people of inland Libya.
"Appal" means to terrify. "Moorish" refers to the people of North Africa under Iarbas's rule.
The "second Paris" is Æneas, compared to the Trojan prince who stole Helen; Iarbas implies he stole Dido as Paris stole another man's wife.
"Forsooth" is an archaic word meaning "in truth," used here sarcastically. "Essenced" means perfumed; "emasculate" means unmanly.
"Dardan" means Trojan, from Dardanus, an ancestor of the Trojans. "Tyrian" means of Tyre, the Phoenician city from which Dido's people came.
His mother Venus promised Æneas would found a great line, and she twice saved him from the Greeks, notably during Troy's fall.
Teucer here is the ancestral Trojan king, not the Greek archer; "Teucer's blood" means the Trojan line.
Ausonian is a poetic name for Italian; Lavinium is the city Æneas will found in Latium, named for Lavinia.
Mercury's rod (caduceus) guides souls to Tartarus, the underworld, and controls sleep and waking.
Cyllene's god is Mercury, born on Mount Cyllene in Arcadia.
Atlas is Mercury's mother's father: Maia, Mercury's mother, was Atlas's daughter.
"His speech clave to his throat" means his voice stuck, so he could not speak; "clave" is the old past tense of cleave, to cling.
A Mænad was a female follower of Bacchus (Dionysus), who roamed mountains in ecstatic frenzy; the sacred emblems and triennial orgies are his festival rites.
"Strip off the mind that clothes you" begs him to abandon his present resolve, as if his purpose were a garment.
Elissa is another name for Dido.
"Bridegroom's torch" refers to the torch carried in a Roman wedding procession; he denies ever formally marrying her.
Grynean and Lycian Apollo refer to his shrines at Grynium and in Lycia, whose oracles Æneas says command him to go to Italy.
Dido denies Æneas divine descent: his mother was Venus and Dardanus, Troy's founder, was Jove's son. Caucasus and Hyrcanian tigers stand for savage, pitiless origins.
Apollo's oracles at Lycia were said to guide Æneas; Dido sarcastically cites the gods' commands he claims compel his departure.
"Aye, of course" is bitter sarcasm: she mocks the idea that gods would trouble themselves over her lover's departure.
She neither detains him nor argues; "refute" means to rebut. It is a contemptuous dismissal.
Teucrians: Trojans, named from their ancestor Teucer.
Careened: turned on one side for cleaning or repair; here, ships being readied for launch.
"Wreathed the sterns": sailors decorated the ships' sterns with garlands, a sign of departure or safe voyage.
Dido lists wrongs she did not commit: joining the Greek (Danaan) league at Aulis, sending ships against Troy (Pergamus), or desecrating Anchises' tomb.
"To confirm her in pursuing her intent" means the omens strengthened her resolve to die; "closing her eyes on the sun" is a euphemism for dying.
Pentheus, king of Thebes, was driven mad for resisting Bacchus and saw doubled suns and a doubled Thebes. The comparison is from Greek tragedy.
Orestes, son of Agamemnon, was pursued by the Furies after killing his mother Clytemnestra. Tragic stage representations are meant.
"Gave conception to the demon" means she conceived the dark, fatal plan; the demon is the thought of suicide.
Atlas, the Titan, was imagined at the western edge of the world holding up the sky on his shoulders.
The Hesperides guarded a tree of golden apples in the far west, with a dragon set to watch it.
Hecate, goddess of witchcraft and the underworld, is triple-formed and identified with Dian (Diana) as moon and huntress.
Avernus was a lake in Italy thought to be an entrance to the underworld; its water suits necromantic rites.
"Nomad bridegrooms" refers to the African Numidian chieftains, such as Iarbas, whom Dido had refused.
Ilion is Troy; Teucrian means Trojan, from the ancestor Teucer.
Laomedon, king of Troy, cheated Apollo and Neptune of their pay for building Troy's walls, so Trojans were proverbial for broken faith.
"The same countenance" means Mercury looks as he did in his first warning; the "second warning" refers to his earlier visit telling Æneas to leave Carthage.
"Infatuate" means foolishly blind to the danger; "the wall of danger" is a figurative barrier closing in.
"Convulsed with ships" means the sea will be churning with Dido's pursuing fleet; "dawn-goddess" is Aurora.
"Hawsers" and "cables" are the thick ropes mooring the ships to shore.
"Propitious stars be ascendant" asks that favourable stars rise, a prayer for good fortune on the voyage.
Aurora, goddess of dawn, was the wife of Tithonus, a mortal she loved; she rises each morning from his bed.
"Flouted" means mocked or treated with contempt; "chance-comer" is a stranger who happened to arrive, as Dido dismisses Æneas.
Dido sarcastically recalls Æneas's famed piety: he carried his household gods from Troy and bore his old father Anchises on his shoulders.
Serving a son to his father as a meal recalls the myth of Thyestes and Atreus, a horror Dido imagines inflicting on Æneas.
Hecate was a goddess of night, witchcraft and crossroads; "Elissa" is another name for Dido.
The "unknown avenger" foretells Hannibal and the Punic Wars between Carthage and Rome; "Dardanian" means Trojan, after Dardanus, ancestor of the Trojans.
A fillet is a ribbon or headband worn by priests and sacrificial attendants.
"Stygian Jove" is Pluto, ruler of the underworld; Dido pretends the pyre is for a rite to end her love, hiding her suicide.
"Presage" means an omen or foreboding; Æneas will see the flames from sea and sense disaster.
"Fame" is Rumour, personified earlier in Book 4 as a monster spreading news.
"Sidon" is the Phoenician city near Tyre, from which Dido's people came; the name here stands for her Phoenician folk.
Proserpine's cutting a lock of hair consecrates the dying to the underworld; without it, Dido's soul cannot leave her body.

context_notes.text: Juno was Carthage's patron goddess and is hostile to the Trojans, so Anna's claim of her blessing is ironic.
Teucrians is another name for the Trojans, after their ancestor Teucer.
Juno, Jove's wife and daughter of Saturn, hates the Trojans and favors Carthage, so she wants Æneas to stay there rather than reach Italy.
Venus knows Juno's real aim is to divert Æneas's destined Italian empire to Libya, so she answers cautiously.
The Queen of Cythera is Venus, whose cult was centered on the island of Cythera.
Apollo spent winters at Lycia and summers on Delos, his birthplace, where he was honored by many peoples in festival.
Ascanius wants dangerous prey like boar or lion rather than timid deer, showing his youthful eagerness.
Dido, queen of Carthage, had vowed loyalty to her dead husband; her union with Æneas is the scandal Fame spreads.
A Mæonian (Lydian) cap with chin straps was Eastern headwear, which Romans viewed as effeminate dress.
Jove sends Mercury, his messenger, because Æneas has lingered with Dido in Carthage instead of sailing to Italy.
Ascanius is Æneas's young son, whose descendants are fated to rule Rome; Jove argues Æneas is cheating him of that.
Æneas wears Dido's gifts, showing how far he has settled into her city and her life.
Mnestheus, Sergestus and Serestus are Trojan captains under Æneas.
Pygmalion, Dido's brother, had murdered her husband, so she fled Tyre; Iarbas was a neighbouring Libyan king whose suit she had rejected.
Priam was the last king of Troy; Pergamus was its citadel.
Juno, queen of the gods, protected Carthage and had arranged the union; Jove, king of the gods, sent the order for Æneas to leave.
The messenger is Mercury, sent by Jove to remind Æneas of his destiny to found a kingdom in Italy.
Anna is Dido's sister and confidante, who had encouraged the affair, so she is a natural go-between.
Dido keeps a shrine to Sychæus, her first husband, murdered by her brother Pygmalion. Her devotion to it makes her remarriage a betrayal.
The Massylians were a North African people; the priestess is a magician from the far edge of the known world.
Dido's pretext is that the pyre will burn everything Æneas left, so that either he returns or she is freed. In fact it will be her funeral pyre.
Sidon is a Phoenician city. Dido's people, the Tyrians, came from Phoenicia and founded Carthage.
Mercury was the messenger of the gods, sent by Jove to remind Æneas that his destiny lies in Italy.
"She" is Dido, queen of Carthage, abandoned by Æneas's planned departure and now contemplating revenge and death.
Dido's own nurse remained in Phoenicia, buried; Sychæus was Dido's murdered first husband, so Barce was his nurse.
The Trojan garments, sword and bed were left by Æneas; Dido has placed them on the pyre.
Dido's brother Pygmalion murdered her husband Sychæus for his wealth, and she later fled Tyre and founded Carthage.
Iris is Juno's messenger and goddess of the rainbow; Juno, patron of Carthage, pities Dido.

literary_notes.text: Love is a wound and a hidden fire consuming Dido, which presents her passion as a slow, physical injury.
Dido's exclamations show agitation and admiration as she begins to confess her feelings.
Her wish that Sychæus keep her heart in the grave shows her loyalty and the strength of the vow she is about to break.
Loosing the ties of honour hints that Dido's yielding will lead to her ruin.
Love is a flame feeding on her bones and a silent wound, picturing passion as a hidden bodily injury.
Dido is compared to a wounded doe fleeing with the arrow still in her side, showing a hidden, incurable wound and her aimless frenzy.
The halted towers and walls reflect Dido's neglected duties; her private passion brings public ruin to Carthage.
Juno's offer is deceitful and Venus sees through it, while neither goddess considers Dido's own interests.
Juno's planned storm and shared cave anticipate the fateful union of Dido and Æneas.
Æneas is compared to Apollo arriving at Delos, stressing his godlike beauty and presence among the hunters.
The sudden storm interrupts the cheerful hunt and anticipates the disaster that will follow from the cave.
Nature supplies wedding signs, yet they are portents of ruin, so the apparent marriage is darkly ironic.
The narrator steps in with a grim judgment, telling the reader that this day begins Dido's death and sorrow.
Fame is given a body, speed and life, turning rumour into a living monster that grows as it travels.
Her head hidden in the clouds while she walks the ground exaggerates how rumour swells from small beginnings.
Feathers, eyes, tongues, mouths and ears together picture rumour as a creature of constant watching and telling.
"Fiendlike goddess" conveys the narrator's moral judgment of Fame.
Iarbas addresses Jove directly, his rhetorical questions expressing angry doubt about the god's power.
Italy's "brood of unborn empires" and a war-cry from its heart present the land as a living, fertile body carrying future power.
Atlas the mountain has shoulders, chin and beard, so the landscape becomes a giant old man.
Mercury's plunge to the sea is compared to a low-flying shore bird, making his descent vivid and graceful.
Mercury mockingly calls Æneas a "fond husband" building his wife's city, shaming him for acting like a consort rather than a founder.
Fame is portrayed as a malicious spirit that whispers in Dido's ear, giving rumor an active, hostile will.
Dido's raving through the city is compared to a Bacchic Mænad, conveying wild, uncontrolled passion.
Dido argues that even Troy would not justify such a perilous voyage, sharpening her accusation of his cruelty.
The wish for a little Æneas to play in her hall makes her loneliness vivid and tender.
The repeated "There is" gives Æneas' declaration of duty a firm, final tone.
Calling his parents a mountain and tigresses figuratively denies his humanity and accuses him of cruelty.
Dido's threat of haunting him foreshadows the lasting enmity between Carthage and Rome.
The Trojans' busy preparations are compared to ants storing grain, stressing their orderly, relentless purpose.
The narrator addresses Dido directly, heightening sympathy for her suffering.
Æneas, unmoved by pleas, is likened to an oak withstanding Alpine winds; his deep roots symbolize duty.
Dido's dream-haunted state is likened to the madness of tragic figures Pentheus and Orestes, raising her suffering to tragic scale.
The reader knows the pyre is for Dido's death while Anna sees only mourning rites, so Anna's trust is painful.
The peaceful sleeping world is set against Dido's wakefulness, which makes her isolation sharper.
Love is described as a sea storm that swells and surges, and her passion becomes a force that overwhelms her.
Dido's string of questions dramatizes her inner conflict as she considers and rejects every possible course.
The torch-fires and burning coast anticipate Dido's pyre and the fire seen from the sea as the Trojans sail away.
Mercury's remark about woman's fickleness shows the gods' dismissive view of Dido and pushes Æneas to act.
"The spark flies from man to man" likens the crew's eagerness to fire spreading, conveying urgency.
The repeated "s" sounds in "strong strokes... sweep" echo the rhythm and swish of oars.
A long periodic sentence delays Dido's cry, building tension as she watches the fleet leave, then breaks into direct speech.
Dido's broken questions show her mind swinging between rage and bewilderment.
Dido bitterly mocks Æneas's famed loyalty and piety, words of praise turned into sarcasm.
Dido addresses the Sun, Juno, Hecate and the Furies as if present, turning her grief into a solemn curse.
The repeated pairs, "coast with coast, water with wave, army with army," give the curse a hammering rhythm of endless hostility.
The palace's uproar is compared to a captured city in flames, magnifying one death into a public catastrophe.
"Thrice" twice marks her failed struggle to rise, making her slow agony vivid.
Iris's saffron wings and trailing colours bring a bright, gentle visual contrast to the bloody death scene.
